Cardiopulmonary exercise testing

A ramp test on a cycle ergometer. Work rises every second until something gives out: the heart, the lungs, or gas exchange. Find what stopped each patient.

THINK THROUGH THE RESULTS

CPET report

Peak values below 80% of predicted are flagged, as are a breathing reserve below 15% and a fall in SpO2 of 4 points or more

INTERPRETATIONDecide what limited this patient, then show the stepwise interpretation

    Teaching thresholds: peak VO2 below 80% predicted is reduced; breathing reserve below 15% means ventilatory limitation; peak heart rate at least 85% predicted means the heart reached its maximum; peak RER of 1.10 or more suggests a maximal effort; VE/VCO2 above 34 is inefficient ventilation; an anaerobic threshold below about 40% of predicted VO2max is low (ATS/ACCP 2003).

    HOW THE TEST WORKS

    Following O2 from air to muscle

    The patient breathes through a mouthpiece while pedaling against a resistance that rises steadily. Each breath is analyzed for flow, O2, and CO2, giving V̇O2, V̇CO2, and V̇E; ECG, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry run throughout. Every link in the chain from lungs to circulation to muscle must keep up, and the first one that cannot stops the test.

    V̇O2 = HR × SV × (CaO2 − CvO2)

    In health the heart is the ceiling: heart rate reaches its predicted maximum and breathing reserve is left over. Cardiac output rises from about 6 to 20–25 L/min, and mixed venous saturation falls from about 75% toward 40–50% as muscles extract more O2. The highest V̇O2 reached is the VO2max (the report calls it peak V̇O2). Even healthy lungs show a wider A-a gradient at peak exercise, and elite athletes can desaturate a few points, because very desaturated venous blood flows through the normal shunt. O2 pulse (V̇O2/HR) tracks stroke volume times extraction, so it is low when stroke volume cannot rise or the blood carries less O2.

    V̇E = 0.863 · V̇CO2 / [PaCO2 · (1 − VD/VT)]

    Ventilation follows CO2 output, first by deeper breaths, then faster ones. RER climbs gradually as the muscles burn more carbohydrate. Above the anaerobic threshold, bicarbonate buffers lactic acid and releases extra CO2, so V̇CO2 and V̇E rise faster than V̇O2 and RER climbs above 1. When buffering can no longer keep up, at the respiratory compensation point, ventilation rises even faster and PaCO2 falls. Dead space volume grows with exercise, but tidal volume grows more, so the dead space fraction VD/VT falls. A high dead space fraction (heart failure, pulmonary vascular disease, lung disease) raises V̇E/V̇CO2: more ventilation is wasted for each liter of CO2 removed. The lungs only limit exercise when V̇E approaches the maximal voluntary ventilation (MVV, about FEV1 × 40). MVV is a measured ceiling that healthy people never reach during exercise, which is why there is no "maximal ventilation" to speak of in health.

    Model details. V̇O2 demand is 3.5 mL/kg/min at rest, plus 150 mL/min for unloaded pedaling, plus 10.3 mL/min per watt, with 45 s on-kinetics. The circulatory limit is HRmax × SVmax (135 mL, so peak cardiac output about 24 L/min) × CaO2 × maximal extraction (60%, mixed venous saturation about 40%); heart rate rises linearly with V̇O2. Once work demands more than that ceiling, the extra is paid for anaerobically, and the test ends when that reserve runs out; a faster ramp piles up work faster, so peak work ends further above what peak V̇O2 predicts. The anaerobic threshold sits at about 40% of the way from rest to the circulatory limit (higher with fitness). RER rises from 0.83 at rest to about 0.97 at AT; above AT, V̇CO2 gains another 0.45 mL per mL of extra V̇O2; past the respiratory compensation point PaCO2 falls by up to 6 mmHg. VD/VT falls from 0.33 at rest toward its peak value. Tidal volume plateaus at 60% of VC, and breathing rate makes up the rest. Predicted V̇O2max = weight × (50.72 − 0.372 × age) for men (Hansen, Sue & Wasserman 1984); predicted HRmax = 220 − age; predicted MVV uses the PFT page's healthy FEV1. Not modeled: blood pressure, ECG, lactate, dynamic hyperinflation, and the slow component of V̇O2.
